analysis.one_liner: Eliminates all federal taxes on profits from selling stocks, businesses, and other assets.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors and died in the Ways and Means Committee without ever receiving a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the tax code so that, starting in 2002, 100 percent of a taxpayer's capital gains — the profit from selling stocks, business interests, real estate, and other assets held over time — could be deducted from income entirely, eliminating the capital gains tax. It would also have repealed the separate lower capital gains rate structure in current law. The bill was referred to the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors who realize large capital gains — a group heavily concentrated among the wealthiest households — would pay zero federal tax on those profits after 2001. Fund companies, REITs, and pass-through businesses that channel capital gains to investors would benefit from increased asset sales and flows.

how_it_helps.text: After December 31, 2001, the bill allows a taxpayer to deduct 100 percent of net capital gain from gross income, effectively eliminating the tax on investment profits [S3].
The bill repeals the existing preferential capital gains rate structure (section 1(h)) and related provisions, replacing them with full exclusion of gains [S3].
Special transition rules cover pass-through entities — mutual funds, REITs, S corporations, partnerships, estates, and trusts — so gains flowing through those structures are excluded as well [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would lose the revenue it currently collects on capital gains, which is paid overwhelmingly by high-income households. That revenue shortfall would have to be made up through other taxes, borrowing, or cuts to public spending.

drawbacks.text: Capital gains income is highly concentrated among the wealthiest households, so a full exemption would direct the overwhelming share of its benefit to them while shrinking federal revenue [S3].
The bill contains no offsetting revenue, so the cost of eliminating the tax would fall on general taxpayers through deficits or through higher burden elsewhere [S3].

Combining a full exclusion with the existing ability to deduct capital losses against ordinary income would create tax-advantaged games around gain/loss timing; the bill only partially limits loss deductions (section 1201 coordination and section 172 changes) [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a broad benefit to holders of investment assets and near-certain large revenue losses, without any offset, and the benefits would be concentrated among the highest earners. From a fiscal standpoint the design was the most aggressive form of capital gains tax relief possible — not a targeted cut but full repeal of the tax — which helps explain why it attracted no cosponsors and no committee action.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Ways and Means Committee in May 1998, and the committee never took it up, so it died quietly when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Scarborough introduced the bill on May 13, 1998 [S1].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee that writes tax law [S5].
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — appears in the action history, and the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No law changed, so the tax treatment of capital gains was untouched. The Treasury kept collecting capital gains revenue it would otherwise have lost, and no one gained anything from the bill itself.

for.name: Rep. Joe Scarborough
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Capital Gains Sunset Act and referred it to the Ways and Means Committee.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: With zero cosponsors and no votes, there was no record of partisan support or opposition beyond the sponsor's own party affiliation.

industries.note: A full capital gains tax exemption would concentrate its benefit on households that realize large investment gains, at the cost of federal revenue that funds public programs.

industries.industry: Mutual funds, REITs, and pass-through investment vehicles
industries.note: The bill includes special rules letting funds, REITs, partnerships, and S corporations pass fully tax-free gains to their investors, which would likely increase asset sales and flows through these vehicles.
